records.title: Marine heat kills about 2.6 million farmed fish on North Gyeongsang's East Sea coast in August 2026
records.description: Prolonged high sea temperatures on North Gyeongsang's east coast killed about 2.635 million farmed fish between 4 and 31 August 2026, about 2.58 million of them olive flounder, with losses of about 2.62 billion won. Pohang accounted for about 2.517 million deaths, and officials feared the year could pass the 2024 record of about 3.005 million. A high-temperature advisory was issued on 3 August and upgraded to a warning on 10 August.

location.name: Pohang, Uljin and Yeongdeok coast
location.detail: North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea, east coast of the Korean peninsula facing the East Sea (Sea of Japan); Pohang had most deaths.

records.layer_rationale: Sustained high coastal sea-surface temperature is the physical driver; the fish deaths are its documented consequence.

notes.harm: About 2,635,000 farmed fish died at North Gyeongsang farms between 4 and 31 August 2026, mostly olive flounder (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Pohang confirmed deaths at 43 land-based farms and losses of about 2.62 billion won; the city supplied oxygen, pumps and ice and released 400,000 juveniles, with no fishery closure (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.scale: Three coastal counties were hit (Pohang, Uljin, Yeongdeok), and the Ministry counted 13.533 million farmed fish dead at 455 farms nationwide by 4 September (ref 1, ref 3).
notes.duration: The 2026 advisory ran from 3 August with water still above the warning threshold on 1 September, after a record of about 3,005,000 deaths in 2024 (ref 1).
notes.significance: A high sea-temperature advisory was issued on 3 August and upgraded to a warning for the Gyeongju-to-Uljin zone on 10 August 2026 (ref 1, ref 2).

population_affected.note: The sources count fish, not people.

key_measure.text: About 2,635,000 farmed fish died on North Gyeongsang's east coast between 4 and 31 August 2026, with losses of about 2.62 billion won (Nocut News, 1 September 2026).

Disaster relief is capped at 50 million won per fish-farming household and insurance uptake is about 40% (ref 3).

records.title: Sea of Japan surface waters hit record warmth in 2024 and stay far above normal in 2025
records.description: Japan's Meteorological Agency reports that sea surface temperature around Japan in 2024 was 1.44 degC above the 1991-2020 average, the highest since 1908, with the Sea of Japan well above normal for most of the year and its northern part the warmest on record for January 2025 (records start in 1982). A September 2024 marine heatwave lifted Sea of Japan surface temperatures up to 5 degC above average, and 2025 was the third-warmest year on record around Japan. Korea's fisheries institute reports the East Sea warmed 2.04 degC from 1968 to 2024, the fastest of the seas around Korea.

location.name: Sea of Japan / East Sea
location.detail: Whole sea, with the Japanese west coast and Korea's east coast; Russian and North Korean waters are not covered in the cited figures.

records.layer_rationale: Basin-scale warming of the sea surface, driven by global warming and a stronger Tsushima Current.

notes.harm: Nippon.com ties the September 2024 heatwave (up to 5 degC above average) to training rainstorms over the Noto Peninsula, and NIFS reported a 21.6% fall in 2024 productivity around Korea, but neither measures harm to the Sea of Japan alone (ref 4, ref 5).
notes.livelihoods: NIFS recorded 143 billion won of aquaculture losses in 2024, the highest since 2012, a national Korean figure not limited to the East Sea (ref 5).
notes.scale: JMA and NIFS figures cover the Sea of Japan as a whole, with the Japanese and Korean shores (ref 1, ref 2, ref 5).
notes.duration: JMA says the 2024 anomaly stayed high for most of the year, 2025 ranked third on record, and the long-term trend is 1.36 degC per century (ref 1, ref 2, ref 3).
notes.significance: JMA issued a formal diagnosis of the record on 5 March 2025 and a long-term trend page last updated 5 March 2026; no enforcement or treaty action (ref 1, ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Sea surface temperature around Japan in 2024 was 1.44 degC above the 1991-2020 average, the highest since statistics began in 1908 (JMA, 5 March 2025).

records.title: Noto Peninsula earthquake lifts the coast by up to 4 m and strands fishing ports
records.description: The 1 January 2024 magnitude 7.5 Noto earthquake raised parts of the peninsula's north coast by about 4 m, exposing seabed and leaving some ports dry. NASA reports about 85 km of coastline affected, about 4.4 square km of new land and more than 15 fishing ports in Ishikawa with uplift. By September 2025 Wajima still relied on temporary piers, and large vessels used Kanazawa about 90 km south. After the 1 January 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake, damage was confirmed at 60 of 69 fishing ports in Ishikawa and the Fisheries Agency listed 20 as unusable in March 2024, mostly in Wajima and Suzu. The seabed around Wajima port rose 1.5 to 2 metres, boats now moor in stacked layers at temporary piers and large vessels use Kanazawa, about 90 km away. The Naoetsu port quay in Niigata was fully restored in March 2025.

location.name: Northern Noto coast, Wajima area
location.detail: Ishikawa Prefecture, Japan, Sea of Japan coast of the Noto Peninsula; Kaiso fishing port and the Port of Wajima are named in the sources.

records.layer_rationale: Tectonic uplift moved the shoreline seaward and drained harbours, a physical coastal change rather than a pollution event.

notes.harm: Uplift of 3.6 to 3.9 m at Kaiso fishing port lifted subtidal oysters, worm tubes and bivalves out of the water, and rocky-shore algae turned white as it dried (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: Seabed around the Port of Wajima rose 1.5 to 2 m, temporary piers were needed and large vessels moved to Kanazawa about 90 km away (ref 2).
notes.scale: The Geospatial Information Authority counted about 85 km of uplifted coastline and about 4.4 square km of exposed land (ref 1).
notes.duration: A September 2025 briefing to Wajima ama divers on the new seabed map and temporary piers still in use show the effects more than a year after the quake (ref 2).
notes.significance: Japan's Geospatial Information Authority measured the uplift and the Japan Hydrographic Association published a before-and-after seabed map of northern Noto (ref 1, ref 2).

population_affected.note: The cited sources describe coast and ports, not a count of fishing households.

key_measure.text: Some areas of the north Noto coast rose as much as 4 m, shifting coastlines and leaving some ports dry (NASA Earth Observatory).

signals: Wajima had Ishikawa's most fishing vessels and largest catch before the quake and now relies on temporary piers (ref 2).
Ama divers have been resurveying changed fishing grounds since heavy rain in September 2024 (ref 2).

corrective_actions: Temporary piers were installed at Wajima unloading sites (ref 2).
The Japan Hydrographic Association and Nippon Foundation resurveyed northern Noto by airborne laser in April to May 2024 and shared trial seabed maps in June 2025 (ref 2).
Temporary piers were built at Wajima and a reconstruction consultative panel was set up on 25 March 2024 (refs 1, 2).
The Umi-no-Chizu project resurveyed Noto waters in April and May 2024 to map the new seabed (ref 2).
The Naoetsu central quay was fully restored by March 2025 (ref 3).

records.title: Gangneung's Haseong Beach rated severely eroded after an underwater breakwater built for a power plant
records.description: South Korea's national coastal erosion survey found 43.3% of surveyed areas at risk or severe, with 138 areas graded C and 18 graded D, and rated Gangneung's Haseong Beach on the East Sea coast severe. The Korea Times reported that an underwater breakwater built in 2020 for the private Anin power plant project accelerated sand loss. A 2026 report put the share of C and D areas above 44%, while the ministry said conditions had improved over the past year.

location.detail: Gangneung, Gangwon Province, South Korea, East Sea coast; national survey figures cover all Korean coasts.

records.layer_rationale: Coastal sand loss from wave action and coastal structures, with sea level rise warned of as a growing pressure.

notes.harm: Haseong Beach was graded severe (D) for erosion, and the Korea Times says the 2020 underwater breakwater accelerated sand loss (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The cited articles report no closures or lost income at Haseong Beach (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.scale: The documented problem is one beach, although the national survey context covers 18 D-grade and 138 C-grade areas (ref 1).
notes.duration: The breakwater dates from 2020, the share of at-risk areas rose from 55.2% in 2017 to 62.4% in 2020, and the 2023 survey and a 2026 report still show erosion (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.significance: The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries grades beaches A to D in an annual survey running since 2001, and Haseong is in the severe class (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Dissolved oxygen is falling from the Sea of Japan's deep water to its shelves, and the sea is projected to acidify fastest around Japan
records.description: Peer-reviewed studies document a long-term decline of dissolved oxygen in the Sea of Japan's deep and bottom water and, since the 1960s, in shallower bank and shelf waters, with part of the Tsushima Strait area projected to reach a sublethal oxygen threshold by the end of this century. Japan's Meteorological Agency projects that the Sea of Japan will see the largest drop in surface pH of any sea around Japan by 2081-2100. The studies were published in 2021 and 2022 and cover records up to the 2000s and 2015.

location.name: Sea of Japan basin and southern shelves
location.type: Deep basin and shelf waters (oxygen and pH)
location.detail: Whole sea; the shelf study covers Yamato Bank, Wakasa Bay, off Awashima and east of the Tsushima Strait, with the deep-water model covering the East/Japan Sea.

records.layer_rationale: Warming-driven weakening of deep-water formation and rising carbon dioxide change the sea's oxygen and carbonate chemistry.

notes.harm: Oxygen declines are documented but no harm is; Ono projects a 134 micromol per kg sublethal threshold in part of the Tsushima Strait area by about 2100 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources reports fishery or coastal-economy disruption from oxygen or pH change (ref 1, ref 2, ref 3).
notes.scale: Kim and colleagues describe the decline across the deep (1500-2500 m) and bottom (2500-3500 m) layers of the whole East/Japan Sea (ref 2).
notes.duration: Ono analysed data from the 1960s to the 2000s and Kim and colleagues cover 1980 to 2015, a multi-decade chronic trend (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.significance: The sources are research papers and a JMA projection, with no formal notice, listing or enforcement (ref 1, ref 2, ref 3).

population_affected.note: Not a population-level finding.

key_measure.text: Oxygen below 300 m in the southern Japan Sea fell by 0.51 to 0.80 micromol per kg per year, comparable with earlier deep-water rates of 0.46 to 0.69 (Ono, Journal of Oceanography, 2021).

trend.note: Oxygen declines since the 1960s are significant in the deep water and, per Ono, spreading upward into shallower layers; the cited records end in 2015 or earlier (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Waste plastic tanks and fishing floats keep washing ashore on Japan's west coast, mostly Korean and Chinese labelled
records.description: Japan's Ministry of the Environment counts about 10,500 to 10,900 waste polyethylene tanks washed ashore a year in FY2023 to FY2025, about 5,250 to 5,900 of them labelled in Korean, plus about 106,600 fishing floats in FY2025, mostly Chinese labelled. Nagasaki (2,654 tanks in FY2025), Yamagata (1,385) and Shimane (1,307) report the most. Tank contents recorded in the tables include oil and strong acid.

location.detail: Prefectures from Hokkaido to Nagasaki, including Tsushima, with language labels pointing to Korean and Chinese origin; Kagoshima and Okinawa are also in the national table.

records.layer_rationale: Large plastic containers and fishing floats arrive from abroad on ocean currents and accumulate on Japanese shores.

notes.harm: The FY2025 tables record tanks with contents on 107 counts, including oil and strong acid in earlier years, which could injure beach users (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited tables report no beach closures or fishery restrictions (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.scale: Counts come from about twenty prefectures along the west and Kyushu coasts, covering a national coastline rather than a site (ref 1).
notes.duration: The ministry has surveyed tanks since FY2008, and counts of 10,497, 10,655 and 10,880 in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 show no decline (ref 1, ref 2, ref 5).
notes.significance: The ministry publishes formal annual prefecture tables under its Sea of Japan mass-landing survey (ref 1, ref 5).

records.title: Sea of Japan autumn-spawning squid stock at a record low, with record-low 2025 quota and a small-boat suspension
records.description: Japan's Fisheries Research and Education Agency assessed the autumn-spawning Japanese flying squid stock, which lives mainly in the Sea of Japan, at a predicted record-low 145,000 tonnes of biomass for the 2024 fishing year, well under the 255,000 tonnes needed for maximum sustainable yield. Trade press reported that the 2025 national quota was cut 76% to a record low and raised 34% mid-season, and in late 2025 small boats were ordered to stop after landing 2,039 tonnes over their allocation.

location.name: Japanese flying squid grounds, Sea of Japan
location.detail: Autumn-spawning stock fished mainly by Japan's Sea of Japan prefectures and by Korea; the national quota also covers the Pacific-side winter-spawning stock

records.layer_rationale: A commercial fish stock depleted below its maximum-sustainable-yield level.

notes.harm: The autumn-spawning stock biomass for the 2024 fishing year was predicted at a record-low 145,000 t, with spawning biomass of 65,000 t against an MSY level of 255,000 t (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Small fishing boats were ordered to suspend operations from November to March after exceeding their quota, and Hokkaido fishers asked for the suspension to be lifted (ref 4); this is a restriction, not the loss of the fishery.
notes.scale: The stock spans the whole Sea of Japan and is fished by Japan and Korea, with Chinese catch assumed by the assessors (ref 1), so it is a regional-sea stock rather than a single bay.
notes.duration: Biomass fell from 2016 to 2019, rebounded briefly in 2020 and has fallen again every year since 2021, while catch dropped from 374,000 t in 2006 to 28,000 t in 2023 (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Fisheries Agency set a record-low 2025 quota, raised it mid-season for the first time since 1998, and a Fisheries Policy Council subcommittee reallocated quota in December 2025 (refs 2, 3, 4).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Japanese flying squid has no international catch limit while foreign catches in the Sea of Japan are poorly known
records.description: The North Pacific Fisheries Commission's 2026 species summary states that its measure for Japanese flying squid sets no catch or effort limits and that the Commission has done no stock assessment, leaving management to domestic rules such as Japan's total allowable catch. Japan's own assessment says Chinese and North Korean catches are not well known and assumes a Chinese catch averaging 150,000 tonnes a year in 2004 to 2020 (excluding three low years), drawing on a 2020 satellite study that counted over 900 Chinese vessels fishing in North Korean waters in 2017.

location.name: Japanese flying squid, Sea of Japan and NW Pacific
location.detail: Squid fished by Japan, Korea, China, North Korea and Russia in the Sea of Japan and adjoining waters; the NPFC covers the Pacific high seas

records.layer_rationale: The gap is in the management regime, with no shared catch limit or assessment.

notes.harm: The NPFC summary says no stock assessment has been conducted for the Convention Area and the autumn stock is recorded as at a record low in Japan's assessment (refs 1, 2), so harm is potential from unmanaged catch.
notes.livelihoods: The cited sources document no closure or restriction caused by the governance gap itself (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The Commission's measure covers several flag states in the North Pacific and the squid straddle Japanese, Korean, Russian and North Korean waters (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: The 2020 satellite study reported Chinese fleets in North Korean waters in 2017 and 2018 (ref 3) and Japan's assessment assumes Chinese catches from 2004 (ref 2).

records.title: Korean east-coast minke whale bycatch trade and illegal whaling under scrutiny after DNA tests find protected whales on sale
records.description: A lawmaker and an environmental federation bought meat from 27 of 115 whale-meat restaurants in October 2026 and DNA tests found 20 minke and seven protected whales (five Bryde's, one sei, one fin), all seven in Busan. Korea Coast Guard data cited by Kyunghyang Shinmun show 33 illegal-capture cases, 148 people and 52 whales from 2022 to August 2026, and a Pohang boat captain was arrested in July 2026 over five minke whales. Bycatch minke whales may be sold legally; one fetched 71 million won at Ulsan in July 2026.

notes.duration: The Coast Guard recorded 50 to 70 minke whales as bycatch each year from 2019 to 2024 and illegal-capture cases cover 2022 to 2026 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Steller sea lions cost Hokkaido fishers about 727 million yen in 2023 as culling continues under a revised policy
records.description: A 2025 Frontiers in Marine Science study cites Hokkaido Government figures that Steller sea lion conflict cost about 727 million yen in 2023 in lost catch and damaged gear, and interviewed fishers in 12 villages on the Sea of Japan and Sea of Okhotsk coasts, most of whom backed population control. Japan's November 2024 report to the World Heritage Committee says the 2024 management policy sets a Sea of Japan upper limit of 511 animals a year and notes the Committee's concern about continued culling.

notes.harm: Hokkaido's management policy allows up to 511 sea lions a year to be taken in the Sea of Japan and the World Heritage Committee raised concern about culling without population data (ref 2); the effect on the population is not quantified.
notes.livelihoods: Conflict cost about 727 million yen in lost catch and damaged gear in 2023, and one Teuri fisher said that if damage worsened the fishery might be impossible to continue (ref 1).
notes.scale: The interviews covered 12 villages on the Sea of Japan and Sea of Okhotsk coasts of Hokkaido (ref 1).
notes.duration: The study describes conflict over decades (ref 1) and the 2012 to 2021 average bycatch of 61 animals is quoted in the 2024 report (ref 2).
notes.significance: The Government of Japan revised its Steller sea lion Basic Management Policy in 2024 after a World Heritage Committee decision (45 COM 7B.84) (ref 2).

records.title: Mitsubishi quits two Akita offshore wind projects in the Sea of Japan and Japan postpones its fourth auction
records.description: On 27 August 2025 a Mitsubishi-led consortium confirmed it would not proceed with three round 1 projects totalling about 1.7 GW, including Yurihonjo (819 MW) and Noshiro-Mitane-Oga (479 MW) off Akita, citing cost increases. The Economy Minister called the decision deeply regrettable, the government plans to re-auction the sites, and round 4 including two Hokkaido zones at Matsumae and Hiyama was postponed from 14 October 2025.

records.description: The Belize-flagged bulk carrier Rubymar was hit by a missile on 18 February 2024 while passing Bab el-Mandeb and sank on 2 March 2024. US Central Command reported an 18-mile oil slick and about 21,000 metric tons of ammonium phosphate sulfate fertiliser aboard, and warned of an environmental risk. The sources in hand are from February to March 2024; no later monitoring of the wreck was found.

records.title: Fuel oil from two wrecked tankers fouls the Kerch Strait, Anapa and Crimea coasts, and a federal emergency follows
records.description: Two Russian fuel-oil tankers, Volgoneft-212 and Volgoneft-239, wrecked in the Kerch Strait on 15 December 2024 and spilled about 2,400 tonnes of fuel oil according to Russia's Transport Ministry. Fuel oil reached the Anapa and Temryuk coasts and Crimea, regional and federal emergencies were declared, and Rospotrebnadzor declared 141 Anapa beaches and nine in Temryuk district unsuitable for recreation. By August 2026 pumping of fuel oil from the sunken tanker sections was reported complete, 111 Anapa beaches had received Rospotrebnadzor approval documents, and courts had ordered owners to pay about 84.9 billion rubles in environmental damage. After two tankers were damaged in a storm in the Kerch Strait on 14 December 2024, the Delfa Dolphin Rescue and Research Center reported 32 dolphin deaths it said were most likely related to the fuel-oil spill, most of them endangered Azov harbour porpoises. Russian authorities said up to 200,000 tons of soil may have been contaminated, and Rospotrebnadzor declared 141 Anapa beaches unfit for recreation, a status its head said still applied in February 2026. Local reports in March 2026 described dead birds and dolphins left uncollected on Anapa beaches.

notes.livelihoods: Swimming bans were posted on Anapa and Temryuk beaches and the governor waived the tourist tax for the year while saying Anapa would be ready for tourists in the next season (ref 3); 111 Anapa beaches had approval documents by August 2026 (ref 1).

records.title: Fuel oil clots from the Kerch Strait tanker spill wash up on the Odesa coast
records.description: In late January 2025 Ukrainian environmental inspectors found fuel oil clots of 0.5 to 5 cm on the Odesa region coast, including a 1.5 km line at Katranka where a sand sample held 10.5% petroleum hydrocarbons by mass, and a petroleum film in Odesa port. The pollution was traced to the Russian tankers wrecked in the Kerch Strait on 15 December 2024. Collection of the clots began on 29 January and the environment ministry asked for wider monitoring and an assessment of risks to coastal nature reserves.

location.detail: Coast of Odesa oblast west and south of Odesa city (Katranka in Lyman community, Kurortne, Mykolaivka in Serhiivka community, Tuzly Estuaries National Nature Park), Ukraine.

records.layer_rationale: Fuel oil from a distant tanker wreck contaminating a national coast.

notes.harm: A sand sample at Katranka contained 10.5% petroleum hydrocarbons by mass (105 g/kg) along a 1.5 km oiled line (ref 1), and about 5,000 dead jellyfish on 2 km of shore were linked to the fuel oil by a Tuzly park biologist (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited reports documents a beach closure, fishing restriction or port stoppage on the Odesa coast; a petroleum film in Odesa port on 28 January is the only port-related finding (ref 1).
notes.scale: Findings are a few shoreline stretches within one oblast, from Katranka to Mykolaivka (ref 1), and on 8 January 2025 the Odesa coast had not been considered at risk (ref 2).
notes.duration: Fuel oil was found from 24 to 30 January 2025 and clean-up started on 29 January, with monitoring ongoing three weeks later (refs 1, 3): weeks.
notes.significance: The Deputy Minister of Environmental Protection ordered stronger monitoring, wider zones and a risk analysis for reserves, and the oblast safety commission met in extraordinary session (refs 1, 3): a formal notice.

Officials put the polluted area at about 10,000 square metres and deployed booms, while the monitoring group Transparent World estimated about 7 square kilometres from satellite imagery. Petroleum products also reached the Tuapse River, though officials described that contamination as localised.

records.title: Record Black Sea marine heatwave in 2024 with anomalies above 4.6 C and events lasting over 30 days
records.description: A Copernicus Marine Ocean State Report chapter published in September 2026 found that the Black Sea and Mediterranean both had record marine heatwave intensities and durations in 2024, with anomalies above 4.6 degrees C along the Anatolian coast and events lasting over 30 days. Turkish marine scientists reported surface water near 27 C in September 2024 against a normal of about 22 C, and Copernicus Climate Change Service recorded record annual sea-surface temperatures for the Black Sea in 2024.

location.name: Black Sea basin, strongest on the Anatolian coast
location.detail: Whole Black Sea; the CMCC study singles out the Anatolian (Turkish) coast, the area west of Crimea and the central and south-western basin.

records.layer_rationale: Marine heatwaves are a physical climate extreme of ocean temperature.

notes.harm: A Turkish ecologist estimated warming may have raised the spread of Mediterranean alien species in Turkish seas by 5 to 6 times and warned warm surface water can reduce oxygen (refs 3, 5), but no mortality event is documented in these sources.
notes.livelihoods: A Karadeniz Technical University professor said anchovy fishing practices should be reconsidered (ref 2), but no closure or catch loss is documented.
notes.scale: The whole Black Sea is affected, with strong events covering more than 80% of the basin in the CMCC analysis (ref 1), which scores as a regional sea.
notes.duration: Events lasted over 30 days and moderate events were detected on more than 125 days in 2024 (ref 1), after a record-hot July 2023 reported by Turkish researchers (ref 5).
notes.significance: The Copernicus Marine Ocean State Report and the Copernicus Climate Change Service report record temperatures (refs 1, 4); no emergency or enforcement action.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Sea snot returns to the Sea of Marmara in 2024 as most promised wastewater plants are still unbuilt
records.description: Mucilage returned to the Sea of Marmara and the Bosphorus and Dardanelles about three years after the 2021 outbreak, with a diver documenting it at 5 to 25 metres depth in the Gulf of Erdek in December 2024. Türkiye's environment ministry says almost 80% of the 169 advanced biological wastewater plants municipalities pledged under the 22-item Marmara action plan were not fully established, and fined four municipalities about TL 9 million in one month in January 2025.

records.layer_rationale: Nutrient-rich wastewater and warm, stagnant water drive mucilage blooms.

notes.harm: A diver documented mucilage at 5 to 25 m in the Gulf of Erdek, and fishers say fish die in large numbers in severe mucilage years (ref 1), but no measured mortality or standard exceedance is reported.
notes.livelihoods: Fishers told Bianet that mucilage sinks and breaks nets, buoys, reels and winches and that they avoid affected areas (ref 1).
notes.scale: The recurrence is reported across the Sea of Marmara, the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles (ref 1), a national sea rather than a single bay.
notes.duration: The first outbreak was in 2021 (ref 3) and it returned in December 2024 and was still reported in January 2025 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The environment ministry fined Istanbul, Bursa, Tekirdağ and Balıkesir municipalities about TL 9 million in one month for discharges (ref 2), an enforcement action.

records.title: Romanian Black Sea waters remain eutrophic, with falling oxygen and rising Noctiluca blooms
records.description: A 2024 assessment of the Romanian exclusive economic zone for 2020 to 2022, based on 68 stations and 617 water samples, found coastal waters carry higher nutrient levels and more algal blooms than offshore water. A 2025 analysis of 1960 to 2023 data on the Romanian coast found rising seawater temperature, falling oxygen and a rising nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio linked to more Noctiluca scintillans blooms.

location.name: Romanian Black Sea coast and EEZ
location.detail: Romanian coast and exclusive economic zone including Danube Delta transitional waters and the northwestern shelf, assessed by the Grigore Antipa institute in Constanța.

records.layer_rationale: Excess nitrogen and phosphorus drive blooms and oxygen loss in coastal water.

notes.harm: Coastal waters need roughly 38% less phosphorus and 37% less nitrogen to reach good environmental status, and the 1960-2023 record shows falling oxygen and more Noctiluca blooms (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Neither peer-reviewed paper reports a fishery or beach restriction tied to the eutrophication findings.
notes.scale: The assessment covers the Romanian EEZ and coast, 68 stations in 2020 to 2022 (ref 1), a national coastline rather than the whole sea.
notes.duration: Eutrophication has affected the Black Sea since the 1980s and the Romanian record runs from 1960 to 2023 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Two peer-reviewed assessments by the national marine institute; no formal notice, listing or enforcement is reported in the opened abstracts (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Romanian Black Sea coast and Danube Delta erode by up to 8 m a year as beach works run over budget
records.description: Reporting by the Balkans and Caucasus observatory OBCT in August and September 2025 says 43% of Romania's coastline is highly sensitive to erosion and 37% is already receding, with the Danube Delta losing up to 8 m a year and peaks of 20 m. A coastal protection programme launched in 2013 with over 840 million euros of EU funding has added beaches and breakwaters between Mamaia and Eforie, and Apele Române defends the shift from nature-based solutions to breakwaters and nourishment.

records.description: Researchers at Tuzly Lagoons National Nature Park recorded 63 dead harbour porpoises on the Odesa Oblast coast between 18 May and early July 2026. The park's research head attributes the deaths to oil pollution and underwater noise from explosions, sonar and missile strikes, while the cited report says the precise causes have not been conclusively established. A specialised environmental prosecutor in Odesa Oblast is investigating the deaths within a criminal case into alleged ecocide.

records.title: Marine heatwaves are becoming more frequent across the Gulf of Guinea, peer-reviewed analysis finds
records.description: A peer-reviewed analysis of satellite and buoy temperatures from 1991 to 2020 found about two marine heatwave events a year in the eastern tropical Atlantic, with frequency rising, most sharply on the northern Gulf of Guinea coast. The longest events lasted roughly 47 to 49 days (2019) and anomalies above 2 C were strongest off the Congo-Gabon coast. A 2025 conference abstract by the same group extends the work to coastal ecosystems in Cote d'Ivoire's Grand-Bereby Marine Protected Area.

notes.harm: The paper does not measure ecosystem damage; it notes heatwaves can cause habitat loss, bleaching and harmful blooms generally, so harm is potential only (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery closure or income loss is documented; the authors only note that the Gulf of Guinea supports Atlantic tuna fishing and upwelling-driven food webs (ref 1).
notes.scale: The analysis covers the whole eastern tropical Atlantic and Gulf of Guinea, a regional sea (ref 1).
notes.duration: Frequency has risen since about 2015 and the longest equatorial and Congo-Gabon events in 2019 lasted roughly 47 to 49 days, a recurring pattern over decades (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Recurrent Sargassum influxes strand on the northern Gulf of Guinea coast and disrupt fishing
records.description: Satellite-based studies show Sargassum biomass in the northern Gulf of Guinea rose significantly from 2011 to 2022, peaking around September with a smaller peak in March to May. A 2026 study finds strandings arrive twice a year, mostly advected from the eastern tropical Atlantic and pushed ashore by winds after Cape Palmas. In Ghana, Sargassum-entangled nets reduce catches and communities have turned to food rationing and loans.

location.detail: Ghana is the documented impact case; Sierra Leone is where spring biomass builds up offshore and Cape Palmas (Liberia) is the entry point for onshore transport.

records.layer_rationale: Floating macroalgal bloom influx linked to sea-surface temperature, salinity and river inputs.

notes.harm: The Phycology study reports no measured ecological damage; stranded biomass and possible metal uptake are flagged as unquantified risks, so harm is potential (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: In Ghana, Sargassum-entangled nets reduce catches at peak months and communities use food rationing, loans and alternative income (ref 1).
notes.scale: The influx affects the northern Gulf of Guinea coast across several countries, a regional-sea scale (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Strandings recur every year since the 2011 influx, with peaks in March to May and September to November (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Peer-reviewed paper and a preprint only; no government notice or emergency declaration is cited (refs 1, 2).

records.title: ICJ rules Equatorial Guinea holds title to Mbanie, Cocotiers and Conga islands in dispute with Gabon

records.title: Studies document large mangrove loss in Nigeria's Niger Delta, with oil spills and invasive nypa palm as drivers
records.description: A University of Galway study reported in February 2025 estimates about 5,644 hectares of Niger Delta mangrove are lost to oil spills each year. records.title: Petrobras drills the Morpho exploration well off Amapá after a contested Ibama licence and a drilling-fluid discharge
records.description: Ibama licensed Petrobras to drill the Morpho well in block FZA-M-59 in the Foz do Amazonas basin in October 2025, after refusing a licence in 2023. Drilling stopped for weeks after an 18.44 m³ discharge of synthetic drilling fluid on 4 January 2026 that Ibama fined at R$ 2.5 million; Petrobras announced oil discoveries in August and October 2026. Federal prosecutors and civil-society groups contest the licence in court, citing reef, spill-modelling and consultation concerns, while Petrobras says it met all of Ibama's requirements. Ibama issued Petrobras an operating licence on 20 October 2025 to drill exploratory well FZA-M-059, about 175 km off Amapa, after a 2023 refusal. records.title: Oil export terminal and floating LNG plans in Golfo San Matías draw a UNESCO request to suspend works near Península Valdés
records.description: The Vaca Muerta Oil Sur pipeline (437 km) is to end at an oil terminal at Punta Colorada, Río Negro, and a consortium plans floating LNG vessels in the same gulf. In July 2026 the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, as reported by Argentine media, asked Argentina to suspend works on the pipeline and terminal until studies show no harm to Península Valdés, citing tanker traffic, whale collisions, noise, lighting and spill risk. Argentina told UNESCO the project has an impact assessment, mitigation measures and a spill contingency plan. At its 48th session in July 2026 the UNESCO World Heritage Committee asked Argentina to suspend works on the Vaca Muerta Sur pipeline and the Punta Colorada oil terminal until studies show no harm to Peninsula Valdes, about 30 km away, citing tanker traffic, whale collisions, noise and possible hydrocarbon spills. A 2025 NOAA GNOME spill model by WCS and the Foro para la Conservacion del Mar Patagonico found that oil would reach the coast within 6 to 8 days in every scenario.

records.title: Avian influenza killed about 97% of southern elephant seal pups at Península Valdés in 2023; the colony fell about 61%
records.description: The 2023 H5N1 avian influenza epidemic killed about 97% of the southern elephant seal pups born that year at Península Valdés, Chubut, and an uncertain number of breeding adults. A WCS Argentina census of October 2024, reported in September 2025, estimated 19,871 animals older than one year, down about 61% from roughly 60,000, and says the population would move from Least Concern to Endangered under IUCN criteria. A Marine Mammal Science study projects recovery to 2022 levels by 2029 to 2051 if only pups were affected, and around 2091 if breeding females were also affected.

records.title: Brazil's extended continental shelf claim over the mineral-rich Rio Grande Rise remains undecided after its ISA crust contract ended
records.description: Brazil asked the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf in December 2018 to recognise its shelf beyond 200 nautical miles on the Brazilian Oriental and Meridional Margins, an area reported to include the Rio Grande Rise about 1,200 km offshore. Meteored reported in July 2025 that the claim had been under review since February 2025 and that the area is treated as common heritage of humankind until decided. The ISA contractor listing shows the sponsored cobalt-crust exploration contract of the CPRM, dated 9 November 2015, ended by voluntary termination effective 27 June 2022.

records.layer_rationale: Jurisdiction over seabed minerals is decided through the UN shelf commission and the seabed authority.

notes.harm: No mining has taken place and the sources document no damage; the USP researcher Luigi Jovane calls for understanding ecosystem services before any use (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or community is reported as affected (refs 2, 3).

notes.duration: The claim dates from December 2018 and is still undecided in July 2025 (refs 2, 4).
notes.significance: A formal CLCS submission was filed on 7 December 2018 and the ISA register lists the exploration contract as ended by voluntary termination in 2022 (refs 3, 4).

records.title: Durban beaches closed repeatedly for E. coli as failing sewage works pollute rivers and the sea
records.description: eThekwini Municipality closed beaches along the Durban coast in January 2025 and again in December 2025 after E. coli contamination and wastewater pump and plant failures. On 18 December 2025 the KwaZulu-Natal High Court found the municipality had failed to prevent sewage spills into its rivers and the ocean and had reopened five beaches without provincial approval. The municipality later put the cost of restoring its wastewater infrastructure at R6 to R8 billion.

location.detail: eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa; Indian Ocean coast from uMhlanga to Amanzimtoti

records.layer_rationale: Untreated sewage and faecal bacteria reach the coast from failing wastewater works and pump stations.

notes.harm: eThekwini detected E. coli in 'significant quantities' at four central beaches in December 2025 (ref 5) and the High Court described levels as 'high', indicating untreated waste (ref 1); no numeric readings are published in the cited reports, so harm is scored as potential health harm.
notes.livelihoods: Blue Lagoon, eThekwini, Country Club and Battery beaches were closed in December 2025 while 19 others stayed open (ref 4); the hospitality association said the closures were 'not a disaster' (ref 5).
notes.scale: The closures affect a handful of beaches inside one metropolitan municipality, about four of 23 bathing beaches at the December 2025 peak (refs 4, 7).
notes.duration: Beach closures for sewage reach back to the April 2022 floods (ref 1) and recurred in January 2025 (ref 6) and December 2025 (ref 4); in August 2026 the city still said it needs R6 to R8 billion to restore its works (ref 8).
notes.significance: A three-judge KwaZulu-Natal High Court bench ruled on 18 December 2025 that the municipality breached NEMA and the National Water Act and ignored at least seven directives (ref 2).

records.title: Cape Town's three marine sewage outfalls face a permit appeal, a flow-limit suspension and an ActionSA challenge
records.description: Cape Town discharges screened but otherwise untreated sewage into the Atlantic through marine outfalls at Green Point, Camps Bay and Hout Bay, under permits issued in 2019 and 2022 to 2023. ActionSA and others appealed the permits, the environment minister suspended the daily flow limits in August 2024 pending appeals, and the appeal was still before an independent panel in December 2025. The City's monitoring reports about 99% of samples within guidelines and says the outfalls do not affect Blue Flag beaches; ActionSA disputes that the permits are being met.

location.name: Green Point, Camps Bay and Hout Bay outfalls
location.detail: Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa; Atlantic coast of the Cape Peninsula

records.layer_rationale: Sewage effluent with nutrients, bacteria and some metals is discharged to coastal waters under permit.

notes.harm: Nine of 1,107 samples (0.8%) from July 2025 to January 2026 exceeded the single-sample enterococci guideline and some metals and suspended solids exceeded limits (ref 5); no ecological harm is documented.
notes.livelihoods: The City says the outfalls do not affect recreational areas or Blue Flag beaches and disputes ActionSA's link to beach closures (ref 4); no closure is documented in the cited reports.
notes.scale: Three outfalls serving one city, which the City says handle 5% of its wastewater (ref 4).
notes.duration: The permits date from 2019 (Hout Bay), December 2022 (Green Point) and January 2023 (Camps Bay) (ref 1) and the appeal remained open in August 2026 (ref 6).
notes.significance: The minister suspended the flow limits on 28 August 2024 pending appeals, and a criminal docket on Hout Bay went to the prosecutor (ref 1); the appeals panel had not ruled by December 2025 (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Of 513 seawater samples taken April to June 2026 around the Camps Bay, Green Point and Hout Bay outfalls, 98.6% met water quality guidelines and seven exceeded allowable bacteria levels (ref 6).

records.title: MV Ultra Galaxy wreck spills more than 500 tonnes of fuel and fertiliser cargo on the West Coast
records.description: The Panama-flagged cargo ship MV Ultra Galaxy grounded near Doringbaai in July 2024 and broke up in storms, and SAMSA said only about 8 tonnes of marine gas oil was removed before the rest of its fuel and fertiliser cargo was lost to the sea. Oil reached mining beaches, Papendorp and Strandfontein, and about 180 people in 12 teams were cleaning a 40 km stretch of coast in February 2025 while the wreck was removed. Oiled wildlife was limited to one dead Cape gannet and one oiled plover in the sources opened.

location.name: Ultra Galaxy wreck, Doringbaai
location.detail: West Coast, Western Cape, South Africa; wreck at Duiwegat south of Brand se Baai, near the Olifants River mouth

records.layer_rationale: Bunker fuel and bagged fertiliser from a wrecked ship contaminated beaches and coastal water.

notes.harm: SAMSA said over 500 tonnes of oil, fuel and fertiliser were lost (ref 3) and oil came ashore along the coast, yet CapeNature found no oiled birds at the Lambert's Bay gannet colony and SANCCOB reported only one oiled gannet carcass and one oiled plover (refs 4, 5).
notes.livelihoods: Oil reached ramps 3, 4 and 7 of the Tormin mineral sands mine and parts of the Transhex area, and clean-up crews of about 180 worked a 40 km coastline (ref 4).
notes.scale: Oiling was patchy along a roughly 40 km section of the West Coast (ref 4), a local rather than regional extent.
notes.duration: The ship grounded in early July 2024 (ref 3), oil re-emerged during wreck removal that began in December 2024, and clean-up was still under way on 7 February 2025 (ref 4).
notes.significance: SAMSA activated its national oil spill contingency plan and the ship's insurer tendered the wreck removal, with removal of material from the seabed under way by February 2025 (refs 2, 3, 4).

records.title: Repeated oil incidents in Algoa Bay and along the Eastern Cape coast oil seabirds and wash up tar balls
records.description: Oil from the MSC Apollo at anchor in Algoa Bay on 7 September 2024 oiled penguins at St Croix Island, and SAMSA investigated the source. In January and February 2026, two fishing vessels burned off Gqeberha and St Francis Bay carrying 14 and 2 tonnes of diesel, and tar balls of unidentified origin were reported on beaches in Algoa Bay, the Garden Route and Struisbaai. Algoa Bay also saw ship-to-ship bunkering spills before 2024, which led South Africa to suspend fuelling there.

records.layer_rationale: Fuel oil and diesel from ships and fishing vessels enter coastal water and affect seabirds.

notes.harm: Six oiled African penguins were found on St Croix Island after the September 2024 spill and SAMSA reported two more uncaptured (ref 1); the spill size was unknown and no slick or beach oiling was seen (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited reports describes a beach, port or fishery closure from these incidents (refs 1, 2, 3, 4).
notes.scale: Tar balls were reported across Algoa Bay, the Garden Route and the Struisbaai region (ref 3), so impacts span more than one bay.
notes.duration: Incidents recur from the 7 September 2024 spill (ref 1) to the 12 January 2026 fire off Gqeberha (ref 2) and the 2 February 2026 sinking (ref 4), with bunkering suspended after earlier spills (ref 1).
notes.significance: SAMSA formally investigated the MSC Apollo leak and coordinated wildlife surveillance with SANCCOB (ref 1), and SANCCOB reported the tar balls to the authorities (ref 3); no enforcement outcome is documented.

records.title: Mass die-offs of octopus, lobster and fish along the Swakopmund and Walvis Bay coast, with low oxygen suspected
records.description: In April 2025 thousands of dead and dying octopuses, crustaceans and small fish washed up between Swakopmund and Walvis Bay, after a similar event near Henties Bay about two months earlier. Residents and the reporting suspected low oxygen from river runoff, sulphur eruptions or a Benguela Nino, but no official cause was reported. Namibia's most recent major red tide was in January 2024, and the northern Benguela is prone to low-oxygen events.

notes.harm: Daily Maverick described 'thousands' of dead or dying octopuses, crustaceans and small fish between Afrodite Beach and Bird Island, and a resident said he had never seen such a die-off on this scale (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited pieces documents a fishery, beach or port closure from the April 2025 die-off (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The die-offs cover a stretch of the central Namibian coast from Henties Bay to Walvis Bay, a local to coastal extent (ref 1).
notes.duration: A major red tide struck in January 2024 (ref 2), a similar die-off occurred about February 2025 south of Jakkalsputz and the April 2025 event followed (ref 1), so episodes recur over more than a year.
notes.significance: Only press reports and an advocacy-group article exist; the cited pieces contain no ministry statement or formal notice (refs 1, 2).

City tests reported in 2019 found E. coli at up to 300 times the guideline in parts of the lagoon.

records.title: Namibia grants an environmental clearance for the Sandpiper seabed phosphate dredging project; the agriculture minister appeals
records.description: Namibia's environment commissioner issued an environmental clearance certificate on 5 August 2026 to Namibian Marine Phosphate for the Sandpiper project, which would dredge phosphate-rich seabed sediments on a concession off Walvis Bay. The fishing federation CNFA, the president and conservation groups have opposed the project, and on 2 September 2026 the agriculture minister lodged an appeal against the decision in its entirety. The company says active mining will not start immediately and depends on further permits and an oversight committee.

location.name: Mining licence 170, off Walvis Bay
location.detail: Namibia, Exclusive Economic Zone off the central coast near Walvis Bay; phosphate sediments at 180 to 250 m depth in the northern Benguela upwelling zone.

records.layer_rationale: A permitting decision and appeal over whether seabed dredging may proceed in a fishing ground.

notes.harm: No mining has begun; critics cited by Mongabay warn dredging could hit spawning grounds and mobilise metals, and a retired marine scientist said risks from heavy metals and uranium were not adequately tested (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The project has not started, so no fishery closure or disruption is documented; the fishing federation CNFA opposes it over potential impacts on fishing (ref 2).
notes.scale: The licence covers about 2,234 square kilometres of seabed and mining would sweep about 1.7 square kilometres a year on average, a single concession (ref 1).
notes.duration: The permitting dispute has run for roughly a decade; the 2021 High Court case and the 5 August 2026 clearance are part of one long process (ref 1).

records.title: Rabies established in Cape fur seals along the South African and Namibian coasts
records.description: WOAH reports more than 100 confirmed rabies cases in Cape fur seals in South Africa and Namibia since 2024, the first known establishment of rabies in a free-ranging marine mammal population, with more than 145 human exposure incidents by May 2026. Mongabay reports that retrospective testing found cases back to 2021 and 2022, and that a July 2025 workshop judged the disease likely endemic and no longer eradicable. No human rabies case from a seal has been recorded by the national institute.

records.title: Foreign-flagged vessel impounded off northern Namibia as officials report more illegal fishing near the Angola border
records.description: The Namibian Navy intercepted the foreign-flagged vessel Fu Yuan Yu 9878 near the northern border with Angola in May 2026; the ministry says it had no valid permit and its AIS had been deactivated, and 22 crew were arrested. The fisheries ministry says more foreign vessels have been detected near the border and that some licensed Namibian vessels also fish illegally. The vessel owner's position was not reported, and the suspects face multiple charges.

location.name: Northern Namibia-Angola maritime border
location.type: Border waters under illegal fishing pressure
location.detail: Namibia, northern territorial waters near the Cunene river mouth and the Angola border; vessel brought to Walvis Bay for court.

records.layer_rationale: Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing removing fish from a national fishery.

notes.harm: The vessel was found with a full net of catch and no permit (ref 1); no stock or habitat damage figure is given.
notes.livelihoods: ADF reports Namibia loses more than $83.7 million a year to illegal fishing and cites more than 18,000 fisheries jobs at risk (ref 3).
notes.scale: The ministry reports increased foreign vessel activity along the northern maritime border, a national-waters issue (ref 2).
notes.duration: ADF described the pattern in July 2025 and the ministry reported continued detections in May 2026 (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The Navy impounded the vessel, 22 crew were arrested and appeared in Walvis Bay Magistrate's Court, and Cabinet approved higher penalties (refs 1, 2).
